The carrier has redistributed port coverage across its PEL2, PEL4, PEL5 and PEL6 loops. Under the changes, PEL2 will replace Tianjin with Ningbo and Busan. PEL4 will reinstate Tianjin and add Dalian, while PEL5 will introduce a call at Rizhao. Ningbo will meanwhile be removed from PEL6. The revised services are: PEL2: One 1,300 TEU vessel operating fortnightly between Nakhodka, Ningbo and Busan. PEL4: One 1,500 TEU vessel operating fortnightly between Vladivostok, Dalian, Tianjin and Ningbo. PEL5: One 1,300 TEU vessel operating fortnightly between Vladivostok, Rizhao and Shanghai. PEL6: Two vessels ranging from 1,500 to 2,200 TEU operating approximately weekly between Vladivostok, Nansha and Xiamen. Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy Port of Long Beach More than 110 U.S. trade associations are urging waterfront employers and union leaders to reach a labor agreement and avert a potentially crippling strike at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, with the latest contract extension set to expire just after midnight Saturday. The warning comes as the Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) and International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 face a critical deadline following more than a year of negotiations over a contract covering approximately 250 port security workers. In a joint statement Friday, the associations called on both sides to remain at the bargaining table, negotiate in good faith and keep cargo moving through the nation’s busiest container port complex. “The Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach already face congestion from near-record import volumes,” the groups warned, adding that a work stoppage would jeopardize holiday shipments, disrupt manufacturing supply chains and restrict U.S. exports. The statement was backed by major organizations including the National Retail Federation, U.S. Chamber of Commerce, National Association of Manufacturers, American Trucking Associations and more than 100 other groups representing retailers, manufacturers, agricultural producers and logistics providers. The associations warned that a prolonged disruption could quickly spread beyond the waterfront, affecting trucking companies, railroads, warehouses and distribution networks nationwide. Container backlogs could take weeks or months to clear even after operations resume, they said. A Small Union With an Outsized Impact Although Local 26 represents only about 2% of the ILWU workforce at the two ports, its members perform security duties at terminals handling a substantial share of Southern California’s container traffic. According to PMA, the six container terminals covered by the dispute account for approximately 85% of cargo at Long Beach and 33% at Los Angeles. The larger concern is that thousands of longshore workers, marine clerks and foremen covered by separate labor agreements could honor Local 26 picket lines, effectively shutting down cargo operations at affected terminals. PMA warned Wednesday that negotiations held November 17 ended with little progress, while the union had already authorized a strike and indicated it was unwilling to extend the current agreement beyond 12:01 a.m. Pacific time Saturday. The two sides were scheduled to return to the negotiating table Friday in a final effort to avert a work stoppage. The more than 110 trade associations urged both parties to pursue a resolution that protects workers, employers and consumers rather than risk a disruption with nationwide economic consequences. articles.summary: The need for joint European action to strengthen competitiveness, through the effective implementation of the Draghi Report, was highlighted by Greece’s Minister of Maritime Affairs and Insular Policy, Vassilis Kikilias, in a speech following the conference of the European People’s Party (EPP) Group. articles.body: Vassilis Kikilias at the EPP: “We Cannot Afford to Lose Any More Time – Joint European Action Is Needed on Competitiveness and Shipping” in Hellenic Shipping News 21/11/2026 The need for joint European action to strengthen competitiveness, through the effective implementation of the Draghi Report, was highlighted by Greece’s Minister of Maritime Affairs and Insular Policy, Vassilis Kikilias, in a speech following the conference of the European People’s Party (EPP) Group. The conference was held in Athens at the initiative of Eliza Vozemberg, Chair of the European Parliament’s Committee on Transport and Tourism. The Minister stressed that Europe’s strength lies in its elected representatives, who understand the needs of their respective societies, noting that European institutions and administrative bodies must listen to their positions and proposals and take them seriously. “This is the soul and the heart of European politics. Great European leaders in the past contributed to the creation of our European family and the building of the European idea, recognising that people, societies and states must be at the centre of our policies. And, of course, there must be an institutional and administrative framework that implements the policies of the elected representatives of European countries.” He added: “The Draghi Report, approximately two years ago, marked a turning point in addressing the issues we Europeans had been raising concerning competitiveness, the cost of goods and the prosperity of European families. We must be particularly careful and decisive in implementing policies that serve these objectives.” Referring to the strategic importance of shipping to the global economy, the Minister said: “Greece accounts for 61% of the European fleet and 20% of the global fleet, while 80% of world trade is transported by sea. This is an extremely important fact in understanding what is at stake today in Europe and around the world. “Unfortunately, there is a war at the heart of Europe and another in the Middle East. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has been disrupted, creating enormous problems for the global economy, as 20% of the world’s oil and 25% of its natural gas pass through it. We are also facing problems with fertiliser supplies. With the war in Ukraine now continuing into its fifth year, we are experiencing even greater difficulties in supply chains, energy and the prices of essential goods. “Therefore, the more we strengthen competitiveness, invest in our ports and shipping, develop our infrastructure and establish an appropriate regulatory framework, the more opportunities we create for growth in our countries, for exporting our products and for prosperity.” As he pointed out, the importance of shipping to national economies and to the everyday lives of European citizens explains Greece’s position on the Net-Zero Framework, both at the IMO and in Europe. “We support the green transition. However, today, liquefied natural gas (LNG) is the transitional fuel, and there is no other available solution, since the quantities of alternative fuels being produced account for just 0.5% of global demand. “We were about to impose an additional financial burden of hundreds of billions of euros on the shipping industry in order to accelerate the green transition using fuels that are not yet available. Had this happened, it would have further fuelled inflation and increased energy and product prices in Europe and across the world. This would have been disastrous for a Europe already under pressure from inflation and facing an energy crisis and a cost-of-living squeeze.” Mr Kikilias went on to discuss the decisive role of ports and their infrastructure in strengthening European competitiveness, stressing: “Our ports are of strategic importance. Why have the United States decided to reinvest in shipyards, shipping, the maritime transportation of energy and ports, and why are China and countries in the East already doing so? Because these sectors will play a decisive role in shaping global power balances and the decisions that will be taken over the next 25 years. “As Europeans, however, we already have this advantage. We have the fleet and we have the ports. This is something we must support. Therefore, when it comes to the Emissions Trading System (ETS), we must take the competitiveness of European ports into account and seek ways to strengthen it, rather than weaken them in comparison with other ports in the Mediterranean or elsewhere in the world.” Concluding his speech, the Minister announced his intention to give shipping a leading role during Greece’s upcoming Presidency of the Council of the European Union, with the participation of representatives of the industry from Greece and across Europe. “As we are due to assume the Presidency of the Council of the European Union in the coming months, I am particularly pleased to announce that we will organise an Informal Meeting of EU Ministers dedicated specifically to shipping. “We will invite the private sector, the President of the Union of Greek Shipowners, Ms Melina Travlou, as well as the leaders of the Greek and European shipping industries, to join you and us – the Members of the European Parliament, members of national parliaments and the Ministry – in meaningful discussions about the future of the sector. “We want to draw on their capabilities so that the many people we represent and support can prosper. This is the way forward, together.” Source: Greek Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Insular Policy 2026-11-21 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Tanker Market: Arabian Gulf Crude Oil Exports Down 27.6% This Year in Hellenic Shipping News 21/11/2026 T he war in Iran has dealt a significant blow to the Gulf oil export markets, with crude oil loading significantly lower over the 10-month period (Jan.-Oct.). In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Banchero Costa said that “in Jan-Dec 2025, global crude oil loadings went up by +1.8% y-o-y to 2,221.1 mln tonnes, excluding all cabotage trade, according to vessels tracking data from LSEG. This year started well, but the trend reversed from March onwards, and global crude oil loadings in Jan-Oct 2026 were down by -5.8% y-o-y to 1,738.8 mln tonnes. Exports from the Arabian Gulf were down by -27.6% y-o-y to 531.3 mln t in Jan-Oct 2026, accounting for 30.6% of seaborne crude trade, down from 39.8% in the same period of last year. From South America, exports increased by +32.5% y-o-y to 238.8 mln t, with a share of 13.7%. Exports from Russian ports (including oil of Kazakh origin) increased by +6.7% y-o-y in Jan-Oct 2026 to 207.8 mln tonnes, or 12.0% of global trade. From the USA, export volumes increased by +8.5% y-o-y to 166.4 mln t in Jan-Oct 2026, a 9.6% share. From South East Asia exports increased by +2.7% y-o-y to 92.8 mln t in Jan-Oct 2026 (but this inevitably also reflects changes in the re-export of Russian origin volumes)”. According to Banchero Costa, “in terms of demand, the top single country seaborne importer of crude oil in Jan-Oct 2026 was Mainland China, accounting for 18.9% of global trade, although the EU27 as a bloc was a larger buyer. Volumes into China declined by -20.1% y-o-y to 328.4 mln t in Jan-Oct 2026. Imports to the EU27 increased by +0.9% y-o-y to 387.8 mln t, accounting for 22.4% of global trade. To ASEAN, imports declined by -9.2% y-o-y to 219.4 mln t (again this includes Russian volumes later reexported elsewhere in Asia). To India, volumes increased +1.5% y-oy to 200.8 mln t in Jan-Oct 2026”. The shipbroker added that “the Arabian Gulf countries (including Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Iraq and Iran) are the single largest seaborne exporter of crude oil in the world. In 2025 they accounted for 39.8% of global seaborne crude oil exports. In the 12 months of 2025, seaborne crude oil exports from AG countries increased by +1.7% to 883.1 mln tonnes, excluding cabotage, after declining by -0.8% y-o-y in 2024. In Jan-Oct 2026, however, Arabian Gulf crude exports collapsed by -27.6% y-o-y to 531.3 mln tonnes, from 734.1 mln t in the same period of 2025, and their share of global seaborne crude trade fell to 30.6%, from 39.8% a year earlier. About 85.8% of volumes loaded in the AG countries in Jan-Oct 2026 were carried in VLCCs, 11.0% were carried in Suezmaxes, and 3.1% in Aframaxes. These proportions increased in recent years in favour of the largest tankers, as Suezmaxes and Afras were diverted to carry more Russian cargoes”. Meanwhile, “the ranking of export terminals has been transformed by the war in the Gulf, with loadings shifting decisively to terminals that can be reached without transiting the Strait of Hormuz. The main crude oil export terminals in the AG are now: Fujairah (137.8 mln tonnes, or 25.9%, in Jan-Oct 2026), Yanbu (104.0 mln t, or 19.6%), Ras Tanura (59.2 mln t, or 11.1%), Basrah (52.6 mln t, or 9.9%), Sohar (49.8 mln t, or 9.4%), Mina al Fahal (36.7 mln t, or 6.9%), Mina al Ahmadi (14.3 mln t), Zirku Island (11.4 mln t), Das Island (6.1 mln t). Ras Tanura, the largest terminal in the world a year ago, has been overtaken by Fujairah and Yanbu, both of which lie outside the Strait”, Banchero Costa said. “In terms of destinations for crude oil shipments from the AG, the focus in recent years has clearly shifted to Asia. In Jan-Oct 2026, the top destination was South East Asia, accounting for 21.6% of the total AG crude exports, narrowly ahead of Mainland China with 21.5%, followed by India with 14.6%, South Korea with 11.0%, Japan with 7.4%. Direct shipments to the USA now account for just 1.8% of AG exports, and direct shipments to the European Union for just 2.2%. Another 6.1% of AG exports are shipped to the Ain Sukhna Terminal in Egypt to feed the Sumed pipeline, and will eventually mostly end up in Europe. In Jan-Oct 2026, the AG countries shipped 114.4 mln tonnes of crude to Mainland China, which represents a -39.4% y-o-y decline from 188.9 mln tonnesin Jan-Oct 2025. Shipments to South East Asia fell by -27.8% y-o-y to 114.9 mln t, from 159.0 mln t in Jan-Oct 2025. The AG also shipped 77.5 mln t this year to India, which represents a decline of -15.4% y-o-y from 91.6 mln t in the same period last year. Volumes to South Korea declined by -28.4% y-o-y in Jan-Oct 2026 to 58.5 mln t. Shipments from the AG to Japan more than halved, down -52.4% y-o-y in JanOct 2026 to 39.4 mln tonnes”, the shipbroker concluded. articles.title: MEPC 85 to confront net-zero divide
articles.summary: The International Maritime Organization’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85) will convene in London from Nov 30-Dec 3 against a backdrop of intensifying pressure to deliver a landmark agreement on shipping decarbonisation, with delegates facing what many observers see as a defining moment for the...
articles.body: MEPC 85 to confront net-zero divide in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 21/11/2026 T he International Maritime Organization’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85) will convene in London from Nov 30-Dec 3 against a backdrop of intensifying pressure to deliver a landmark agreement on shipping decarbonisation, with delegates facing what many observers see as a defining moment for the sector’s climate transition. The meeting follows a year of difficult negotiations over the organisation’s proposed mid-term greenhouse gas reduction measures. While the committee’s agenda spans a broad range of environmental issues – including ballast water management, amendments to MARPOL and the NOx Technical Code, marine plastic litter, underwater radiated noise and maritime digitalisation – climate policy is expected to dominate proceedings. Central to those discussions will be efforts to resolve outstanding differences over draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI and the package of mid-term measures envisioned under the IMO’s 2023 greenhouse gas strategy. According to the IMO, delegates will consider the outcomes of recent intersessional negotiations and seek ways to address “remaining concerns” surrounding the proposed measures, which combine technical and economic elements intended to accelerate emissions reductions from international shipping. The committee is also expected to continue work on the IMO’s Life Cycle GHG Assessment framework. The significance of the discussions has been heightened by the unresolved fate of the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework (NZF), which environmental organisations argue is the industry’s best opportunity to establish a global mechanism for driving down emissions. Adopt ‘as is’ The Clean Shipping Coalition (CSC), representing environmental non-governmental organisations engaged in IMO negotiations, has urged member states to finalise and adopt the framework before the end of the year. “In order to fulfil the goals of the IMO’s GHG Strategy and to protect our global climate, the IMO and all its member states must adopt the Net-Zero Framework ‘as is’, without further diversion,” said Lukas Leppert, president of the Clean Shipping Coalition. “The product of years of negotiations, the Net-Zero Framework reflects findings from the IMO’s Comprehensive Impact Assessment, is a long-negotiated compromise that brings together a multitude of interests and positions, and is supported by a broad majority.” The coalition argues that the framework, originally approved during MEPC 83 in April 2025, already provides a balanced pathway for implementing the IMO’s decarbonisation objectives. The proposed package combines a global fuel standard with an economic mechanism designed to incentivise lower-carbon fuels and technologies. Adoption was delayed after opposition from a group of member states prevented final approval in October 2025. Environmental groups contend that subsequent attempts to replace or significantly revise the framework have failed to attract broad support. “Since October 2025, when IMO member states voted to adjourn the adoption session for one year, various alternative proposals to the NZF were introduced and intensively discussed, but were neither able to demonstrate a comparable reduction in emissions nor gather sufficient support,” Leppert said. “These alternative proposals aimed at supplanting or distracting from the NZF have fallen away, proving the NZF as the best course ahead.” The CSC frames MEPC 85 as a test of the IMO’s ability to convert years of negotiation into binding regulation. “There is no longer time for going in circles; every IMO member state must get behind the Net-Zero Framework and adopt it before the year ends,” Leppert said. EU stance Shipping industry representatives have also taken a view on how member states should proceed. Ahead of the London meetings, Melina Travlos, president of the Union of Greek Shipowners (UGS), warned that political divisions risk undermining efforts to secure a workable global solution. In a statement, she criticised the European Union’s negotiating stance and argued that flexibility remains essential if consensus is to be achieved. “Two months after the inconclusive last round of negotiations at the IMO on reducing greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping, and with the next critical negotiating meetings approaching, there remains no evidence of positive tangible progress,” Travlos said. She argued that recent discussions at European level had demonstrated an unwillingness to compromise, adding that “the EU’s uncompromising position is steering the IMO process to a new dead end, effectively torpedoing the negotiations by depriving them of the flexibility necessary for any chance of success.” The Greek shipowners’ organisation has consistently advocated a global regulatory framework that recognises differing operational realities across shipping segments and trading patterns. Rather than focusing predominantly on alternative fuels, Travlos called for a broader approach incorporating operational and technical efficiency measures. “For a regulation to be effective it must be pragmatic, proportionate and implementable, while reflecting the commercial and operational realities and constraints of the industry,” she said. Travlos further argued that policymakers must align climate ambitions with technological readiness and fuel availability. “This means taking into account the availability, scalability and affordability of alternative fuels, technologies and supporting infrastructure, as well as competing demand from other sectors,” she said. “Such a regulatory framework must also recognise the diversity of solutions available to the shipping industry, rather than focusing exclusively on alternative fuels. It should support all effective pathways to emissions reduction, including technical and operational efficiency measures.” The contrasting positions highlight the challenge awaiting delegates in London. Environmental groups are pressing for rapid adoption of a framework they view as the culmination of years of climate negotiations, while shipowners and several member states are emphasising practicality, flexibility and the risks of imposing measures that outpace technology deployment and fuel availability. After more than a year of delays, MEPC 85 offers member states an opportunity either to bridge their differences and advance a global climate framework or risk prolonging uncertainty over the sector’s pathway to net zero. Central to those discussions will be efforts to resolve outstanding differences over draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI and the package of mid-term measures envisioned under the IMO’s 2023 greenhouse gas strategy.
The committee is also expected to continue work on the IMO’s Life Cycle GHG Assessment framework.

articles.body: How SAL and DNV are strengthening heavy-lift shipping in International Shipping News 21/11/2026 F rom classification and newbuilding support to operational tools and advisory expertise, SAL and DNV have been collaborating for decades. The partnership supports both the development of SAL’s Orca Class vessels and day-to-day operations, including more efficient cargo planning using DNV’s Route-Specific Cargo Calculator. With a current fleet of 22 DNV-classed heavy-lift vessels, SAL Heavy Lift is a leader in the segment. The Harren Group company’s latest newbuilding programme has set a new benchmark for performance, operational flexibility, and efficiency. Three of a series of five 14,600 dwt Orca Class ships have been delivered so far. SAL is discussing additional newbuilds of the same type with Wuhu Shipyard in China. “Our long-standing collaboration with SAL and Harren Group has covered many different aspects of their fleet,” says Jost Bergmann, Business Director MPV & General Cargo Ships at DNV. Bergmann, who supports SAL’s newbuilding programme for DNV, recently attended the christening of MV Patricia, the third vessel in the series, in Rostock. “The Orca vessels stand out in several respects, both in their design and in how they are intended to support SAL’s operations.” Heavy-lift vessel design built on decades of operational experience The design of SAL’s Orca Class heavy-lift vessels draws on decades of experience in project cargo shipping with a focus on the most demanding cargoes. Developed by SAL’s in-house ship engineering team, the basic design combines the company’s shipbuilding expertise with lessons from operating heavy-lift vessels and transporting complex and oversized cargo. The optimized hull form supports good seakeeping and helps limit acceleration forces acting on the cargo, which can reduce lashing requirements. A forward deck house protects deck cargo from the elements while enabling long cargo, such as wind turbine blades, to extend beyond the stern. Flexible cargo handling for oversized project cargo Cargo flexibility was also a priority. The vessels’ high freeboard helps protect cargo from water, while DNV’s Hatchcoverless class notation allows oversized cargo to be transported in the open hold. A box-shaped single cargo hold and hatch covers designed for loads of up to 10 tonnes per square metre provide additional options for positioning heavy and oversized project cargo. SAL’s requirements for loading flexibility were considered during the design process. DNV’s class-independent Maritime Advisory experts carried out global structural analyses using the vessels’ three-dimensional finite element model to validate these requirements and develop recommendations for optimizing the design. This combination of vessel design and structural analysis supports the operational flexibility required for complex heavy-lift and project cargo. The Orca Class vessels also have a high ice class rating of 1A and Polar Code certification for operations requiring particular care in low ambient temperatures. Electric cranes and flexible propulsion for heavy-lift shipping The vessels combine their cargo capabilities with new crane, energy management, and propulsion technologies. Two fully electric Liebherr Maritime LS 800 E cranes, each with a lifting capacity of 800 tonnes, provide a combined lifting capacity of up to 1,600 tonnes in tandem operation. Using electric rather than hydraulic cranes also eliminates the risk of hydraulic oil escaping from the crane system. A hybrid energy management system combines gensets with lithium-titanium-oxide batteries to optimize energy use. Shore power capability allows the vessels to operate without on-board emissions when suitable infrastructure is available in port. Methanol-ready propulsion for greater fuel flexibility The Orca Class also features a dual-engine concept designed for different operating profiles. One engine supports normal cruising, while the second main engine can provide additional power through the gearbox when required, enabling speeds of up to 18.5 knots for time-critical cargo deliveries. The vessels are designed to be methanol-ready, except for the tanks, allowing conversion for operation with green methanol. Safety and accessibility are also integrated into the design, with stairs providing access to walkways, entrances, accommodation, work areas, and cargo areas. Operational excellence supported by DNV The cooperation between SAL’s parent company Harren Group and DNV extends beyond newbuilding projects. For vessels in operation, Harren Group draws on DNV’s digital class services, software, and class-independent Advisory expertise to support day-to-day fleet management and address technical challenges. My Services on Veracity, for example, gives superintendents and inspectors a central overview of their vessels, helping them monitor the fleet, plan upcoming activities, and arrange surveys easily. Integrated port state control guidance, including relevant checklists and authority focus areas, also helps crews prepare vessels for inspections and smoother port stays. Jan-Hendrik Dammann, Fleet Manager, Harren Shipping Services GmbH & Co. KG, confirms: “DNV’s digital solutions, especially My Services on Veracity, are the benchmark in the market and a real asset in our day-to-day work. For our ships in service, DNV is a partner we can rely on.” The cooperation also gives Harren Group access to DATE (Direct Access to Technical Experts), connecting the company directly with DNV experts when technical questions arise. “We’ve been partners with DNV for a long time, and what we value most is the quality of support and service we receive, online and in person,” highlights Dammann. “We can reach the right experts when needed, and our requests are handled quickly and competently. This close and straightforward cooperation means we usually find joint solutions that are practical and work for both sides.” DNV’s Route-Specific Cargo Calculator delivers solid monetary benefits Carrying extremely heavy or oversized project cargoes comes with stowage restrictions and sea-fastening challenges. Securing breakbulk cargo on board in compliance with the IMO Code of Safe Practice for Cargo Stowage and Securing (CSS Code) requires engineering expertise as well as costly sea-fastening equipment and often comes with considerable efforts for deck reinforcements. Intended to predict the acceleration forces acting on the cargo during transit, the CSS Code assumes the harsh conditions in the North Atlantic, and uses standardized ship contours. But for trips in much more benign sea areas, these rules are overly conservative. While calculating the more realistic accelerations along a given route takes expert knowledge, DNV’s Route-Specific Cargo Calculator tool on Veracity provides a convenient, user-friendly way for cargo planners to predict the acceleration forces during the relevant season without requiring engineering skills. Increased stowage flexibility and capacity utilization SAL is using the tool more and more, says Karsten Behrens, Managing Director at SAL Engineering. “It gives us greater stowage flexibility compared to the CSS Code, for example in matching the vessel with the cargo or placing cargo on the weather deck. It also reduces the lashing effort and expense. These effects can multiply when identical cargo is transported along the same route repeatedly.” In one case, the tool helped SAL make better use of the available space on board by calculating a reduced route- and season-specific maximum transverse acceleration of 3.95 m/s2, which is roughly 75 per cent of the assumed value according to the CSS Code of 5.23 m/s2. The resulting reduction of deck loads allowed 15 to 20 per cent more cargo to be transported on that voyage. “In some cases the DNV tool allows us to accept a particular shipping order; in other cases, it reduces the number of trips we must take,” says Behrens. “This is in the best interests of both the cargo owner and the ship operator.” Stored digital ship model reduces lashing time and effort The Route-Specific Cargo Calculator uses a digital model of the ship that has to be entered into DNV’s Veracity system only once. All the user has to enter for a specific trip are some loading condition parameters like draft, trim, and metacentric height (GM), the stowage positions of cargo items, plus the route and, optionally, the season. The tool uses its database of route-specific sea states to return realistic acceleration values. “While we could calculate these values ourselves at SAL Engineering,” remarks Behrens, “the DNV tool reduces the effort and speeds up the process, freeing up our resources for other purposes.” Another typical use case is transporting wind turbine components from the U.S. East Coast to Mexico. The CSS Code would require extensive lashing, but sailing this route during the summer season reduces the lashing requirement by about 50 per cent. RSCC unlocks operational potential and strengthens risk management “The DNV tool helps open up untapped potential,” explains Behrens. “What is more, even in the North Atlantic in winter, when we operate under the most severe conditions, the tool gives us reassurance that the sea-fastening and loading measures we take are on the safe side. For shipments with our newbuild MV Elise, we not only knew that we were on the safe side, but the tool even told us how far.” Source: DNV, https://www.dnv.com/expert-story/maritime-impact/how-sal-and-dnv-are-strengthening-heavy-lift-shipping/ Tops 2026-11-21 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: The partnership supports both the development of SAL’s Orca Class vessels and day-to-day operations, including more efficient cargo planning using DNV’s Route-Specific Cargo Calculator.
With a current fleet of 22 DNV-classed heavy-lift vessels, SAL Heavy Lift is a leader in the segment.

Peter Sand, Xeneta Chief Analyst: “Offered capacity is increasing on all fronthauls out of the Far East to Europe and the US, with average spot rates unsurprisingly continuing to soften – with one exception. The trade from the Far East to the Mediterranean is moving in mysterious ways, with spot rates increasing 6.8% in the past week. “Average spot rates into the Mediterranean are now USD 1,551 per FEU higher than into North Europe. The fact that this widening spread is being driven by increases in the already-elevated rates into the Mediterranean adds to the mystery. “The reason the Mediterranean trade is behaving differently to other fronthauls may be found in the Red Sea, where the ramp-up in services transiting the Bab el-Mandeb Strait since August tailed off in November. “Container ship transits through the strait increased from 305 in August to 463 in October. That trend has now turned, with the seven-day average falling 28% from a peak of 16.6 transits per day on 25 October to 11.9 on 19 November. “Something has happened to cool the return of container shipping services to the Red Sea in November. Whatever the reason, disruption in the Red Sea is felt more acutely on trades between the Far East and the Mediterranean because they are the most operationally exposed to the region. “This is a timely reminder to shippers that the path to forecasted falling freight rates in 2027 will not be plain sailing. articles.summary: After several weeks of improving confidence, recycling buyers are beginning to have second thoughts about how aggressively to pursue fresh tonnage. Bangladesh’s recent optimism has been tempered by weaker steel, political unrest and sluggish domestic demand, prompting some buyers to reconsider their purchasing ideas...
articles.body: GMS Week 47 – The Tide Of Second Thoughts in Weekly Demolition Reports 21/11/2026 After several weeks of improving confidence, recycling buyers are beginning to have second thoughts about how aggressively to pursue fresh tonnage. Bangladesh’s recent optimism has been tempered by weaker steel, political unrest and sluggish domestic demand, prompting some buyers to reconsider their purchasing ideas or delay commitments. Elsewhere, sentiment remains selective rather than distressed. Recycling indications are unchanged across all four destinations, although the shortage of available candidates continues to restrict fresh business. Dry freight surrendered part of last week’s gains, with the Baltic Dry Index easing from 3,020 on November 12 to 2,901 on Thursday, November 19. Capesizes declined to 4,514 and Supramaxes slipped to 1,814, while Panamaxes edged higher to 2,132. Despite the correction, employment opportunities remain sufficiently attractive for many ageing vessels, limiting the incentive for owners to consider recycling. Crude oil continued its downward trajectory, with Brent trading around USD 90 per barrel on Friday and WTI near USD 82. Recovering Middle Eastern exports and expectations of greater supply have outweighed continuing regional security concerns. Lower energy costs may provide some relief to recyclers and steel producers, although uncertain Gulf trading conditions continue to influence vessel employment and disposal decisions. Regional steel markets offered mixed signals. Bangladesh plate retreated from last week’s improvement, while Indian steel recovered towards Friday and Pakistani prices strengthened marginally. Chinese quotations weakened further. These movements have provided little justification for stronger recycling bids, particularly where domestic finished-steel consumption remains disappointing. Bangladesh faces the week’s most challenging domestic developments, with political unrest, disruptions in the garment sector and weak local demand prompting greater buyer caution. India continues to pursue specialist opportunities and has sought Italian support for European approval of selected recycling facilities. Pakistan remains measured, while Turkey faces subdued steel demand and continuing production disruption at a major mill. Waterfront activity nevertheless continued. Alang and Chattogram recorded further arrivals and deliveries, while Gadani received another bulker. These movements primarily reflect previously secured tonnage rather than fresh transactions. No new recycling sales were reported during the week. The market therefore enters the final weeks of November with buyers reassessing their positions rather than abandoning them. Bangladesh’s earlier enthusiasm has given way to greater caution, while India, Pakistan and Turkey remain selective. Owners, meanwhile, still have sufficient trading alternatives to resist recycling. The price board has not moved, but the conviction behind it is being tested. For now, the market is not changing its prices. It is having second thoughts about paying them. articles.body: Drewry: World Container Index Down 3% Last Week in International Shipping News 21/11/2026 For many years, World Container Index (WCI) has been the go-to, independent, global reference for index-linked contracts. If your organisation requires regional visibility/coverage beyond the eight trade lanes provided below, contact the team. Our detailed assessment for Thursday, 19 Nov 2026 • The Drewry World Container Index (WCI), the benchmark widely referenced by procurement teams, decreased 3% to $4,176 per 40ft container this week due to declining rates on the Transpacific trade route. Despite the decline, the WCI remains 126% higher YoY. • On the Transpacific trade route, rates continued their downwards trend for the seventh consecutive week. Rates from Shanghai to New York decreased 9% to $8,194 per 40ft container, the lowest in 15 weeks, and those from Shanghai to Los Angeles fell 5% to $7,026 per 40ft container, the lowest in 12 weeks. In response to the weak demand, carriers are reducing capacity through blank sailings. According to Drewry’s Container Capacity Insight, ten blank sailings have been announced for next week, compared with four this week. Despite these capacity reductions, Drewry expects freight rates to decrease further next week. • On the Asia-Europe/Med trade route, rates from Shanghai to Genoa increased 6% to $4,436 per 40ft container after remaining stable for three consecutive weeks, while Shanghai to Rotterdam rates remained unchanged at $3,496 per 40ft container. Carriers are managing capacity through blank sailings, and according to Drewry’s Container Capacity Insight, four blank sailings are announced for next week, lower than five this week. As demand is expected to strengthen in December ahead of the new contract season, many carriers have announced PSS, ranging from $1,000-1,600 per 40ft container on Asia-Europe/Med effective December. Hence, Drewry expects rates to increase in the coming weeks. • The East-West container shipping market remains under pressure, with different trends on Transpacific and Asia-Europe/Med trade routes. Asia–Europe demand is expected to strengthen in December ahead of the new contract season and Chinese New Year, prompting carriers to push rate increases through surcharges, whereas easing Transpacific demand is likely to drive rates lower. Meanwhile, worsening North Europe port congestion is delaying empty-container returns to Asia, raising concerns over future equipment shortages. Suez Canal transits improved to 57 vessels last week, while only four vessels crossed the Strait of Hormuz. With geopolitical uncertainty and potential labour disruptions at Los Angeles and Long Beach remain key risks, shippers should expect continued rate volatility. articles.title: The Week in Alt Fuels: The net-zero bargain
articles.summary: The IMO faces a difficult choice next month. A softer version of the Net-Zero Framework could help break the negotiating deadlock. But weaker rules could undermine the very transition it is meant to support. The IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) will reconvene from 30 November to 3 December to...
articles.body: The Week in Alt Fuels: The net-zero bargain in International Shipping News 21/11/2026 The IMO faces a difficult choice next month. A softer version of the Net-Zero Framework could help break the negotiating deadlock. But weaker rules could undermine the very transition it is meant to support. The IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) will reconvene from 30 November to 3 December to consider proposals ranging from stronger economic measures to removing greenhouse gas (GHG) pricing altogether. Liberia, Tuvalu, Brazil and a four-country group comprising Australia, Canada, South Africa and the UK have submitted proposals for discussion at the IMO’s intersessional GHG working group meeting from 23 to 27 November. Japan has submitted a proposal calling for softer fuel intensity targets and direct contributions, but it was not circulated within the six-month period required under MARPOL for adoption at MEPC 85. The EU and Pacific Island states support adopting the text approved in April 2025. The US and several other countries, including major oil producers, want substantial changes to its technical and economic provisions. US President Donald Trump has openly opposed global emissions pricing. “There is no global government – and while I am President, there will be no global taxes,” he said. The question is no longer simply whether governments can agree on a global framework, but whether the compromises needed to secure that agreement could leave shipping with rules too weak to drive meaningful change. The case for compromise The Union of Greek Shipowners (UGS) has urged Brussels to show greater flexibility in negotiations. “The EU’s uncompromising position is steering the IMO process to a new dead end, effectively torpedoing the negotiations by depriving them of the flexibility necessary for any chance of success,” UGS president Melina Travlos said. Travlos said Greece and three other EU member states, collectively representing 70% of the EU-controlled fleet, had pressed for the EU to approach the IMO talks with a genuine willingness to negotiate. While she did not name the three countries supporting a compromise, Cyprus, Greece, Malta and Italy called for “realistic, globally applicable and cost effective” regulations during a ministerial meeting in Limassol in September. The four EU countries agreed to work towards the “widest possible consensus” on global measures that support shipping’s green fuel transition while keeping the sector competitive. All four countries supported the framework’s approval in April 2025. Nine shipping industry associations, including BIMCO, ICS, IBIA and WSC, have called for an “achievable, enforceable, and stable regulatory framework” that reflects fuel costs and availability. “The regulatory framework must support credible transition pathways for existing ships and technologies. Continued industry investment and effective implementation will depend on global regulatory certainty and the reliable production and cost-competitiveness of alternative fuels at scale,” the statement said. The associations also stressed the need to avoid overlapping regional and international requirements, including multiple charges on the same emissions. Travlos has made a similar argument, questioning whether the EU values its own regional measures, and the revenues they generate, more than a global agreement. Charles Whitfield, chairman of Australian ammonia developer NH3 Clean Energy, expects IMO member states to reach an agreement in December, although he expects it to be less stringent than the April 2025 version. “But I think that there will be a piece of paper or an agreement that does actually get ratified,” he told ENGINE. Whitfield believes a common international framework would be preferable to the different regulatory approaches emerging across the EU, China and Singapore. But at what cost? Critics of a softer framework argue that political compromise could come at the expense of meaningful emissions reductions. Weakening emissions targets or making compliance payments too cheap could undermine the IMO’s climate goals and slow the shift to cleaner marine fuels, according to a report by University College London’s Shipping and Oceans Research Group and the Rocky Mountain Institute. The Clean Shipping Coalition has urged governments to adopt the framework without further changes. It argues that the existing text already represents years of negotiations and that alternative proposals have yet to demonstrate comparable emissions reductions or attract sufficient support. The proposed IMO Net-Zero Fund is intended to support cleaner technologies, infrastructure and capacity-building, particularly in vulnerable countries. The availability of financial and technical support could help least developed and developing economies manage the transition. Em Fenton, senior director of climate diplomacy at Opportunity Green, has cautioned against reopening the existing compromise. “The Net-Zero Framework represents a hard-fought multilateral compromise. Any significant shift away from this text risks harming not only the level of emissions reductions that can be achieved from such a regulatory measure, but also the justice and equity of its implementation,” they told ENGINE. “Further delay or weakening of the text only serves fossil fuel interests and does nothing to support climate vulnerable countries during shipping’s transition,” Fenton added. A deal worth having? Important questions remain unresolved, from lifecycle emissions accounting and chain of custody to GHG pricing and the proposed net-zero fund. A weaker agreement could bring more governments on board and give shipping a common regulatory starting point. But if compliance becomes cheaper than switching fuels, that certainty may do little to encourage investment in cleaner alternatives. In other alt fuels news this week, South Korea’s Lotte Fine Chemical and Norwegian shipping company Höegh Autoliners plan to expand green ammonia bunkering operations across South Korean ports. Japanese shipping company NYK Line has unveiled a newbuild gas carrier equipped with an ammonia dual-fuel two-stroke main engine at Japan Marine United’s Ariake Shipyard in Kumamoto Prefecture. French energy firm TotalEnergies has shelved its planned $16 billion green hydrogen and ammonia production project in southern Chile, citing weak demand for green fuels and higher-than-expected production costs. Source: By Konica Bhatt, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news/ 2026-11-21 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Iran War Oil Premium Evaporates as Global Crude Supplies Surge
articles.summary: The price of US sour oil has plunged, as a surge in crude supply from Venezuela, Canada and the Middle East gives refiners ample barrels to choose from.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Shutterstock/Sven Hansche By Nathan Risser and Yongchang Chin (Bloomberg) –The price of US sour oil has plunged, as a surge in crude supply from Venezuela, Canada and the Middle East gives refiners ample barrels to choose from. US medium sour export grade Mars traded at a record premium to benchmark West Texas Intermediate futures in the early days of the Iran war. Buyers turned to the Gulf of Mexico variety, which is similar in quality to Middle Eastern crude, as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupted supplies. Now, as oil markets begin to settle after a volatile year, Mars has fallen to a deep discount, making it cheaper for US refiners built to process heavier crude. Mars has dropped from a $10 premium to a $4 discount to WTI futures in less than a month. That’s the steepest discount since late September. Mars rallied to record premium of $17.50 at the peak of supply disruptions in March and April. At the start of the year, before the US and Israel launched their war in Iran in late February, the grade largely traded at a discount. Rising production of heavy-sour crude in Venezuela and Canada has pushed global prices lower in recent weeks. US refiners, major buyers of heavier oil along the Gulf Coast and in the Midwest, have benefited from increased supplies from Canada and Latin America. At the same time, higher shipping costs are weighing on prices at the barrel’s origin by making overseas sales more expensive. Flows from the Persian Gulf have also increased. Higher Middle Eastern flows, however, have reduced the incentive for Asian refiners to take advantage of falling Mars prices, with the US grade still uneconomical to import, according to traders familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named because they aren’t authorized to speak to the media. On a delivered basis to Northeast Asia, Mars for February was priced at a premium of about $12 to $13 a barrel to the Dubai benchmark — around $10 more expensive than similar quality oil from Saudi Arabia, they said. At least one other seller of Middle Eastern crude has also slashed offer prices, they added. “Incremental supply looks to be dominated by heavier and more sour barrels, especially out of Canada, Venezuela, and the Middle East,” Valero’s head of crude supply Randy Hawkins said in an October earnings call. It’s a “race to the bottom” Phillips 66’s executive vice president of marketing and commercial Brian Mandell said on a call with analysts the same month. In Canada, the pipeline that takes oil sands crude from inland fields to export markets on the West Coast is operating at a record 960,000 barrels a day this month, 8% above its stated capacity. Oil will also be shipped on 34 vessels out of the Westridge terminal near Vancouver in November, up from 31 in October. While cheaper heavy crude is a boon to refiners who are already making record profits from the Iran war’s disruptions to global fuel markets, it is coming at a cost to heavy oil producers. “We’re basically going to have to be a price taker,” oil driller Sable Offshore Corp. chief executive office Jim Flores said earlier this month. Sable pumps heavy oil off the coast of California. For now, US crude exports of both heavy and light grades continue at historically elevated levels. US crude exports averaged 4 million barrels a day over the past four weeks, below the weekly record of more than 6 million set in April but well above the 3 million average since the US lifted its crude-export ban in 2015. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.body: DP World has announced an expanded investment of US$ 200 million in the Port of Maputo, following a meeting between Group Executive Chairman H.E. Essa Kazim and Mozambique’s President, H.E. Daniel Chapo. The figure raises the company’s original commitment of USD 165 million and supports its ambition to strengthen Mozambique’s position as a strategic trade and logistics gateway for Southern Africa. The meeting focused on expanding operations, exploring further investment in trade infrastructure and improving transport and logistics links with neighbouring markets. The expanded project will nearly triple the container terminal’s annual handling capacity, from 225,000 TEU to 650,000 TEU by the second quarter of 2027, exceeding the original target of 530,000 TEU. It will let the terminal accommodate larger vessels, improve operational efficiency and reinforce Maputo’s role as a regional logistics hub. DP World operates the Maputo container terminal and is a shareholder in the Maputo Port Development Company, which holds the port concession until 2058. Beyond the port, Maputo is emerging as a multimodal gateway linking Southern Africa’s industrial and agricultural heartlands to global markets, and DP World is strengthening these connections through cross-border road and rail networks and its inland logistics hub at Komatipoort in South Africa. Its Shipping Solutions business is also due to launch a new weekly China-Africa Link later this month, connecting Shanghai, Ningbo, Nansha and other Chinese ports with Maputo and other regional gateways, which together will make the Maputo Corridor a more competitive route for regional trade. Essa Kazim said Mozambique has an opportunity to become one of Southern Africa’s most important trade gateways, and that the ambition is not simply to move more cargo through Maputo but to connect businesses across the region to global markets through better infrastructure, shipping services and inland logistics, helping Mozambique capture more of the value of regional trade.

REUTERS/Stringer Another tanker was struck by a projectile and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, extending a wave of attacks on commercial shipping that has pushed maritime security incidents to their highest weekly level since mid-October. The latest incident occurred at approximately 1500 UTC, eight nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, according to UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) Warning 214-26 . The tanker was transiting outbound through the strategic waterway when an unknown projectile struck its port bow, sparking a fire onboard. The vessel’s company security officer reported no casualties or environmental impact. Authorities are investigating. The attack comes amid a sharp escalation in threats to merchant shipping across the Middle East and Black Sea. According to maritime security analyst Martin Kelly of Orbital Risk Intelligence, shipping experienced 15 attacks and piracy-related incidents over the past seven days, a 50% increase from the previous week and the highest weekly total since mid-October. In the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman, Kelly recorded seven strikes involving six vessels. Four tankers were hit within 13 nautical miles of Khasab over three days, including the LPG tanker TARA GAS , which was attacked twice. The violence has left two seafarers missing and 13 injured, according to Kelly’s assessment. Among the most serious incidents was the November 17 attack on the tanker NAVIG8 MESSI , which suffered a fire after being struck 13 nautical miles north of Khasab. ADNOC confirmed that one crew member was missing and 11 others were injured. The remaining crew were evacuated and the vessel was reported under tow. The TARA GAS , meanwhile, was disabled by a projectile strike on November 16 before being hit again the following day, resulting in another fire and the vessel being abandoned. The pattern points to an increasingly dangerous concentration of attacks along the southern shipping lanes off Oman’s Musandam Peninsula, particularly against tankers attempting to leave the Persian Gulf. The deteriorating security situation is taking a continued toll on commercial traffic. In its weekly maritime security overview published Friday , UKMTO reported 115 outbound and 148 inbound transits over the preceding seven days, down from 139 outbound and 169 inbound crossings the previous week. Combined traffic remains approximately 65% below pre-conflict levels. UKMTO recorded six verified attacks across the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf during its latest reporting period, which covered incidents through November 18. Four occurred in the Strait itself and two in the wider Persian Gulf. Two vessels required assistance, while the outcomes of four others remained unknown. The agency cautioned that its figures do not capture every incident, as some reports cannot be independently verified. Since the U.S.-Iran ceasefire agreement expired on August 17, UKMTO has recorded six total vessel losses, while 22 vessels required assistance and 31 were confirmed to have continued their voyages. The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) continues to assess the threat to commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz as SEVERE , warning that further deliberate attacks are highly likely. The surge in maritime violence extends well beyond the Middle East. Six commercial vessels were struck in the western Black Sea over the past week, according to Kelly, including two ships that sank in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone on consecutive days. The general cargo ship BETUL 8 sank on November 16, followed by the LPG tanker GAS HUSKY on November 17. All 31 seafarers aboard the two vessels were rescued. Maritime security firm Ambrey separately confirmed reports of six vessels struck since November 13, including four attacked near the Sulina anchorage in Romanian waters and two in Bulgarian waters. Ambrey assessed the attacks as part of an escalating Russian campaign involving unmanned aerial and surface vessels. The incidents have raised growing concerns about the safety of commercial shipping in waters adjacent to NATO member states Romania and Bulgaria. Piracy-related activity has also increased in the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean. During the week, a tanker reported being approached by an armed skiff carrying a ladder approximately 430 nautical miles east of Socotra, Yemen. In another incident off Al Mukalla, armed guards aboard a cargo vessel fired a warning shot to repel an attempted boarding. A further incident was reported Friday, when six armed men aboard a skiff fired four shots at an eastbound bulk carrier approximately 95 nautical miles southwest of Al Mukalla. The ship’s security team returned warning shots, forcing the attackers to retreat. No injuries or damage were reported. The incidents underscore the growing range of threats facing merchant vessels, from projectile and drone attacks in active conflict zones to renewed piracy activity along established trading routes. With attacks concentrated around the Strait of Hormuz and the western Black Sea, maritime security analysts warn that the coming week could bring further strikes against commercial vessels. articles.summary: South Korean shipbuilder Samsung Heavy Industries and U.S. nuclear technology company Tesser Atomics have signed an exclusive agreement to develop a nuclear-powered LNG carrier intended for commercial service between the...

Join the leading maritime news network Illustration: Shutterstock South Korean shipbuilder Samsung Heavy Industries and U.S. nuclear technology company Tesser Atomics have signed an exclusive agreement to develop a nuclear-powered LNG carrier intended for commercial service between the United States and Europe. The memorandum of understanding, signed November 19, establishes Samsung Heavy Industries as the exclusive shipbuilding partner and Tesser Atomics as the exclusive reactor technology partner for the demonstration project, which aims to develop the world’s first nuclear-powered LNG carrier. The collaboration brings together Samsung’s ship design and construction capabilities with Tesser’s advanced reactor technology as the companies work toward demonstrating nuclear propulsion on an established commercial trade route. At the center of the project is Tesser’s Triton reactor, a compact fluoride-salt-cooled high-temperature reactor designed specifically for marine applications. The system uses TRISO nuclear fuel and low-pressure molten salt coolant, with a design that allows refueling while the reactor remains in operation. The companies say the technology could provide the power needed to propel large oceangoing vessels without relying on conventional marine fuels. “Demonstrating nuclear propulsion on an LNG carrier crossing the Atlantic would open new horizons for decarbonizing the shipping industry,” said Kyunghee Kim, Executive Vice President and Head of the Future Business Division at Samsung Heavy Industries. The project builds on Norway’s NuProShip research program, which evaluated advanced reactor technologies for merchant vessels, and is being advanced through SFI SAINT, a research consortium led by the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) and supported by the Research Council of Norway. The Norwegian initiative is targeting several nuclear-powered vessel demonstrations in the early 2030s, including an LNG carrier project backed by shipowner Knutsen OAS. Samsung Heavy Industries is no stranger to nuclear-powered LNG carrier development. In September 2025, the shipbuilder and the Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute secured Approval in Principle from ABS and the Liberian flag state for a separate LNG carrier concept powered by a 100-megawatt-thermal molten salt reactor. The latest agreement represents another step toward moving nuclear propulsion beyond conceptual designs and into commercial demonstration. However, significant hurdles remain. Nuclear-powered merchant ships face complex requirements involving reactor licensing, maritime safety, port access, crew training, insurance and liability. The International Maritime Organization is currently working to modernize its regulatory framework for nuclear-powered ships, with adoption of a revised Nuclear Code and amendments to SOLAS Chapter VIII targeted for 2030. The economics also remain uncertain. An ABS-supported study published in October found that a nuclear-powered LNG carrier could cost roughly 2.5 times as much to build as a conventional vessel, although lower fuel costs could improve its long-term economics. For now, the Samsung-Tesser agreement remains a development partnership rather than a firm shipbuilding order. The companies have not disclosed a construction schedule, vessel specifications, project cost or financing arrangements. Still, the project adds to growing efforts by shipbuilders, reactor developers and maritime regulators to determine whether nuclear propulsion can become a commercially viable alternative for deep-sea shipping. REUTERS/Ints Kalnins SINGAPORE, Nov 20 (Reuters) – US Treasury Department officials met with government authorities in Singapore and Malaysia this week, including regulators and national security bodies, to warn of potential risks they could face if they do not comply with US sanctions on Iran. Washington is urging the countries, as well as law firms and banks operating there, to stay alert for Iranian front companies, as it steps up efforts to enforce sanctions in Asia and bring about a speedy end to the conflict in the Middle East. The US is urging additional scrutiny on “high-risk” sectors such as maritime transport, aviation services and procurement networks, “to make sure they’re not fronting for Iran,” said a Treasury Department official. “We want it to be understood too, that we’re going to target these lifelines, and it’s not going to be a negotiation when we find a lifeline that needs to be targeted,” the official said. Since the US and Israel commenced strikes on Iran in February, the US has intensified actions to throttle Tehran’s business interests overseas. In August, President Donald Trump’s administration launched Operation Economic Outcast, resulting in a barrage of sanctions against targets spanning Canadian digital currency platforms to a major Russian banking group. OIL ON WATER For years, tankers have regularly made stops in the waters around Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia to make ship-to-ship transfers of Iranian oil that help obscure its origin. Last year, Malaysian authorities said they would more tightly enforce rules around these transfers and in February seized two tankers and their cargoes. Since April, the US Navy has imposed a blockade on shipping reaching Iran through the Strait of Hormuz, and this month has cracked down on movement over Iran’s land borders and through the Caspian Sea. In July, the Treasury Department sanctioned dozens of individuals, vessels and companies based in Singapore, Hong Kong, the UAE, the Marshall Islands and St Kitts and Nevis linked to Iranian oil magnate Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani. These efforts were starting to disrupt Iran’s source of revenue, the US official said, citing data showing that the country is currently undergoing the worst GDP contraction in four decades and the highest rate of inflation since World War II. However, the official said there was still work to be done. “There’s an Iranian airline that flies to Malaysia, or has, recently, so we raised this,” the US official said, without naming the carrier. Using public flight records, Reuters identified a regularly scheduled flight between Tehran and Kuala Lumpur operated by Iran Airtour, which flew as recently as November 14. A scheduled flight on November 17 did not depart, the records also show. Iran Airtour did not respond to an emailed request for comment sent outside of business hours on Friday. Most Iranian airlines largely stopped flying to Malaysia in 2022 due to US sanctions on refueling Iranian planes. However, Iran Airtour, a privately owned airline, resumed flights to Malaysia in November 2025, according to Iranian media. On September 8, the US imposed sanctions on dozens of companies in the UAE, Britain, Malaysia, Turkey and Kazakhstan it said were supporting Iran’s aviation sector to move weapons, personnel and illicit cargo. The following day, Iran Air officials met with Malaysia’s ambassador to Iran to discuss resuming direct flights between Iran and Kuala Lumpur. Both Malaysia and Singapore implement UN Security Council sanctions on Iran. Singapore’s government said in a statement it “is firmly committed to doing our part” and “preventing bad actors from abusing our corporate vehicles,” citing its efforts to strengthen vigilance in the maritime and financial industries this year. The Malaysian government did not respond to requests for comment. Image courtesy Carnival Corporation Carnival Corporation has signed a contract with Italian shipbuilding giant Fincantieri for two next-generation cruise ships, marking a shift toward smaller vessels designed to reach more destinations. The agreement, valued at more than €2 billion ($2.2 billion), calls for construction of two dual-fuel cruise ships at Fincantieri’s Marghera shipyard in Italy, with deliveries scheduled for 2033 and 2035. Each vessel will measure approximately 130,000 gross tons and feature around 1,650 passenger cabins. The ships will primarily operate on liquefied natural gas (LNG) and incorporate advanced environmental and digital technologies. Unlike Carnival’s recent focus on increasingly massive cruise ships, the new class is being designed with greater operational flexibility in mind, allowing the company to serve ports and destinations that may be inaccessible to its largest vessels. Carnival Cruise Line President Christine Duffy said the new ships will complement the company’s existing fleet of 29 vessels. “With a 29-ship fleet, we know our guests appreciate choices,” Duffy said. “They love the incredible experiences and amenities on our Excel Class ships, the largest in our fleet, but they also love the intimacy our smaller ships offer.” Fincantieri said the design has also been developed as a multi-brand platform, potentially allowing Carnival Corporation to adopt the same basic vessel design across several of its cruise lines in the future. Fincantieri+2 The order comes as Fincantieri is already building three much larger Ace-class cruise ships for Carnival at its Monfalcone shipyard. Those vessels, measuring approximately 230,000 gross tons and capable of carrying nearly 8,000 passengers at full capacity, are scheduled for delivery in 2029, 2031 and 2033. Construction of the first ship, Carnival Destiny, began in July 2026. The latest order therefore represents a significant departure from the industry’s trend toward ever-larger cruise ships. At approximately 130,000 gross tons, the new vessels will be about 43% smaller by gross tonnage than the Ace-class ships. Carnival Corporation CEO Josh Weinstein said the company now has 12 ships on order for delivery through 2039 across its Carnival Cruise Line, Princess Cruises and AIDA Cruises brands. The company is also expanding its private destination infrastructure, including two additional phases at Celebration Key on Grand Bahama, scheduled for 2028 and 2030. Together, the expansions will increase the destination’s land-side guest capacity by 6,000. The latest contract extends a relationship spanning three decades between Carnival and Fincantieri. The Italian shipbuilder has delivered 76 vessels across Carnival Corporation’s brands, including 15 for Carnival Cruise Line. articles.title: IMO Finds Just $10.5 Billion in Maritime Climate Finance
articles.summary: A new study by the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has identified just $10.5 billion in direct maritime climate finance over a six-year period, accounting for only 0.14% of global climate...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network FILE PHOTO: By Mr Nai / Shutterstock A new study by the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has identified just $10.5 billion in direct maritime climate finance over a six-year period, accounting for only 0.14% of global climate finance flows, highlighting a significant funding gap as the shipping industry faces mounting pressure to decarbonize. The findings, released Thursday , come from the IMO’s Maritime Climate Finance Landscape report, which tracked investment between 2018 and 2023 across shipping, ports, alternative fuels and other maritime activities. The study, developed in collaboration with Climate Policy Initiative under the IMO’s GHG-SMART Programme, found that maritime climate finance has grown substantially but remains far below the investment needed to meet the industry’s long-term emissions targets. Annual financing reached $4.7 billion in 2023, representing a compound annual growth rate of 49% over the study period. However, much of that growth was driven by a relatively small number of large projects, raising questions about whether the increases can be sustained. The report estimates that decarbonizing international shipping and developing the supporting shore-based infrastructure will require between $1.2 trillion and $1.6 trillion in capital investment by 2050. The study found that most tracked climate finance flowed into port infrastructure and alternative fuel production, while investments in vessel technologies, shipbuilding and recycling received considerably less attention. In 2023 alone, alternative fuel production and distribution attracted $2.5 billion, while port infrastructure and operations received $1.4 billion. Together, those two categories accounted for approximately 83% of direct maritime climate finance that year. Across the full six-year period, port infrastructure accounted for 39% of tracked financing, followed by alternative fuel production and distribution at 24%. Maritime operations and technologies received 11%, while shipbuilding and recycling accounted for just 0.02%. Public and private investors contributed roughly comparable amounts, although commercial debt dominated the financing landscape, accounting for 61% of tracked flows. Grants represented just 12%. The findings underscore a central challenge facing shipping’s energy transition: investments in cleaner vessels, alternative fuel production and port infrastructure must move forward together. Shipowners need confidence that alternative fuels will be available before committing to new vessels, while fuel producers and ports need assurances that sufficient demand will exist to justify major infrastructure investments. The report also highlights significant disparities in access to maritime climate finance, particularly among small island developing states (SIDS) and least developed countries (LDCs). Although those countries received approximately 68% of tracked maritime climate adaptation finance between 2018 and 2023, primarily for port resilience projects, they accounted for just 1.5% of maritime climate mitigation financing. Almost no tracked financing reached those countries for alternative fuel production and distribution, leaving them largely dependent on international public funding and concessional loans. The IMO said greater coordination between governments, financial institutions and industry will be necessary to improve access to capital, particularly in countries where maritime transport provides a critical link for trade, food, fuel and essential supplies. The study also acknowledged important limitations in the available data. Domestic public spending and private investment in ship retrofits, energy efficiency and shipbuilding are not consistently captured, meaning the $10.5 billion figure should not be interpreted as a complete accounting of all maritime decarbonization investment. The IMO called for more consistent definitions of maritime climate finance, stronger reporting systems and better coordination of investment-ready projects to help direct additional funding into the sector. articles.summary: A Maltese-flagged bulk carrier ran aground on France’s Atlantic coast early Friday after being driven toward shore by strong winds and heavy seas, prompting the helicopter evacuation of 19 crew...

Join the leading maritime news network The Maltese-flagged bulk carrier MIRO G sits aground on a beach near Lit-et-Mixe in southwestern France on November 20, 2026, after being driven ashore by strong winds and heavy seas. A Maltese-flagged bulk carrier ran aground on France’s Atlantic coast early Friday after being driven toward shore by strong winds and heavy seas, prompting the helicopter evacuation of 19 crew members and a major maritime emergency response. The 169-meter MIRO G grounded near Lit-et-Mixe in southwestern France’s Landes region shortly after midnight on November 20, after its crew reported difficulty maneuvering in deteriorating weather. According to France’s Atlantic Maritime Prefecture, the vessel alerted the CROSS-A Étel rescue coordination center Thursday evening after encountering heavy swell and strong crosswinds. The crew attempted an emergency anchorage, but wind gusts reaching 48 knots caused the vessel to drag anchor and drift toward shore. Following the grounding, a French Air and Space Force search-and-rescue helicopter operating from Cazaux evacuated 19 of the vessel’s 22 crew members. The captain and two other mariners remained aboard to assist authorities with the ongoing response. French authorities have since shifted their attention to the possibility of refloating the vessel. A French Navy evaluation and intervention team was deployed by helicopter to assess the ship’s condition and determine whether it can be safely pulled free. Meanwhile, the emergency towing vessel Abeille Bretagne departed Brest in anticipation of a possible refloating operation. A French Navy Falcon 50 maritime surveillance aircraft has also been monitoring the grounded vessel. Authorities said its initial aerial assessment found no evidence of pollution. However, the operation faces significant challenges. According to AFP, the vessel is carrying more than 100 tonnes of diesel fuel, presenting a potential pollution risk. French maritime officials said options under consideration include pumping fuel from the vessel to reduce its weight before attempting to tow it into deeper water. The operation is complicated by rough weather, including waves reaching five to six meters, and difficult access to the beach. The MIRO G , a 2011-built Handysize bulk carrier with a deadweight capacity of approximately 28,200 tonnes, was sailing without cargo when the grounding occurred. The ship was reportedly bound for Rouen, France, where it was scheduled to load approximately 30,000 tonnes of wheat destined for Libya. The incident triggered the activation of Level 3 of France’s ORSEC maritime emergency response system, as well as the Franco-Spanish Biscaye Plan, a bilateral agreement coordinating maritime rescue and pollution response in the Bay of Biscay. The Spanish emergency towing vessel Sar Gavia was also mobilized under the agreement. French authorities have formally instructed the shipowner to take necessary measures to eliminate immediate and future dangers and minimize any potential environmental damage. As of Friday, no pollution had been detected, and the maritime prefecture said operations remained underway. November 20, 2026 © Hatenboer-Water Hatenboer-Water has started building a new headquarters in Schiedam, driving the first foundation pile on Thursday after early demolition work. Due to finish in the third quarter of 2027, the new building project adds manufacturing space and twice the company's current testing capacity as orders grow across shipping and offshore energy. Hatenboer-Water's existing premises in Schiedam have reached their limit. Rebuilding on site upgrades its engineering workshops and manufacturing facilities and keeps the business inside the Port of Rotterdam maritime cluster. Schiedam's focus on maritime manufacturing puts the company close to European shipbuilders, engineering firms and offshore service providers. The site also serves as the main hub for regional offices in Aberdeen, Dubai, Houston, Singapore and Hamburg. Doubling production and testing capacity means Hatenboer-Water can build more systems and run several demanding tests simultaneously, cutting waiting times and speeding up delivery. Inside, the building includes new production equipment, a better layout for moving materials, shared meeting spaces for visiting clients, and upgraded IT infrastructure and access controls. Separate, fully secured office zones with restricted access will let teams work on confidential projects. Designed as an all-electric, fully insulated building, it will also operate without natural gas. Daily operations will not stop during construction. Using a phased 'chessboard' plan, the existing building will stay in use while the first new sections are built. Staff and equipment will move across step by step as each part finishes, keeping production and support running as normal through 2027.
