articles.body: Vice Adm. Burdian appointed as DHS Joint Task Force-Maritime Director Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 Vice Adm. Jo‑Ann Burdian. Image courtesy USCG Vice Adm. Jo‑Ann Burdian was presidentially appointed as the director, Department of Homeland Security Joint Task Force–Maritime (JTF-M), effective Nov. 10, 2026. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin nominated Burdian as director of JTF-M, in accordance with 6 U.S.C. § 348(b)(3)(A), to ensure the critical, continued role of JTF-M in synchronizing multi-agency maritime operations and securing the nation’s maritime borders. “Vice Admiral Burdian’s appointment as the JTF-M director marks a pivotal moment for our collective maritime defense," said Mullin. "Her unmatched operational expertise is critical as JTF-M continues to dismantle illicit networks, prevent hostile exploitation of our maritime borders, and leverage the MOC-P construct to achieve departmental unity of effort and drive nationwide success." JTF-M synchronizes DHS component operations, intelligence, and investigations across the maritime domain to secure U.S. borders, prevent and respond to homeland security crises and facilitate regionally based joint operations. As the DHS Maritime Operations Coordination Plan (MOC-P) program office, JTF-M enhances coordination among DHS components, eliminating redundancy and increasing effectiveness through 35 Regional Coordinating Mechanisms (ReCoMs). These ReCoMs execute DHS missions at every major U.S. port, along all U.S. coastlines and approaches to maritime borders of the U.S. and its territories. The ReCoMs help prevent terrorist, criminal, and hostile activities and dismantle illicit networks attempting to exploit the maritime domain and reduce vulnerabilities while safeguarding legal trade and travel. "I am honored to lead the dedicated staff of Joint Task Force-Maritime as we strengthen our borders and streamline interagency response," said Burdian. "Through our 35 ReCoMs and strong partnerships with the Department of War, we will continue to safeguard legal trade and travel while remaining an impenetrable barrier against cross-border smuggling, illegal immigration and illicit trafficking." Burdian also serves as commander, Coast Guard Atlantic Area and commander, Coast Guard Defense Force East, providing Coast Guard forces and operations across all mission areas from the Arctic Ocean to the Arabian Gulf in support of the DoW and combatant commanders for national defense missions.

articles.title: Energy-Saving System for Marine Generators Touts 10% Fuel Savings
articles.summary: NYK Line, MTI Co., Oshima Shipbuilding, Terasaki Electric and Daihatsu Infinearth have verified the energy-saving performance and operational safety of the Hz Controller System, an energy-saving system for marine generators developed through joint testing.
articles.body: Energy-Saving System for Marine Generators Touts 10% Fuel Savings Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 Copyright Xavier MARCHANT/AdobeStock NYK Line, MTI Co., Oshima Shipbuilding, Terasaki Electric and Daihatsu Infinearth have verified the energy-saving performance and operational safety of the Hz Controller System, an energy-saving system for marine generators developed through joint testing. General sales of the system will now begin. Building on their joint research, the five companies will expand deployment beyond NYK-operated vessels, promoting installation on newbuildings and retrofitting on existing ships owned by other shipowners. The System reduces power consumption and generator fuel consumption by lowering the generator frequency while maintaining the performance required by onboard equipment. This is possible because onboard equipment such as pumps and motors that operate in conjunction with the power supply frequency is designed to deliver the required performance even under anticipated severe conditions and may therefore have excess capacity during normal navigation. Specifically, the System switches between the regular frequency and a lower energy-saving frequency according to shipboard conditions within the range specified by ship classification rules. It utilizes generator frequency control technology (Patent Number JP6238600) that is jointly patented by NYK and Tsuneishi Shipbuilding. Demonstration tests confirmed an approximately 10% reduction in generator fuel consumption compared with operation at the regular frequency. Subsequent verification on an increasing number of vessels equipped with the system confirmed a similar reduction. For general sales, Terasaki Electric will be responsible for the design and supply of the System, while Daihatsu Infinearth will expand its lineup of generator engines compatible with the System.

REUTERS/Stringer By Weilun Soon Nov 20, 2026 (Bloomberg) –A cargo of Iranian crude was transferred between two tankers in the Persian Gulf this week, as the US warned its navy could target vessels that carry out the practice while enforcing a maritime blockade. A US-sanctioned Suezmax called Olym transferred oil to the medium-range Hao Fan on Tuesday, according to nonprofit group United Against Nuclear Iran and data analytics platform Kpler. UANI said Hao Fan, which is not blacklisted by Washington, is spoofing its location near Oman’s Shinas. The tankers turned off their transponders during the operation, which UANI said took place just south of Iran’s main oil export terminal on Kharg Island, deep in the Persian Gulf. It is the first observed transfer since the US reinstated its blockade of Iranian ports in mid-July, said Charlie Brown, an adviser to UANI. The group based its analysis on satellite images and ship-tracking data. The US military issued a notice on Wednesday that it was widening the scope of its blockade to target ships receiving cargoes at sea. The American operation has brought Iranian oil exports to a halt , forcing production curbs and cutting off a key source of revenue for the Islamic Republic. Read More: Iran’s Main Oil Terminals Remain Empty as US Blockade Bites Some small shipments of Iranian liquefied petroleum gas have left the Middle East since the blockade was reinstated, but Brown said it’s unlikely the crude loaded onto Hao Fan is destined for global markets. The vessel took about 200,000 barrels in the ship-to-ship transfer, too little to make an export voyage economic, he added. “Things have been consistent so far with regard to the blockade,” said Brown. The timing of the US notice and the transfer between Olym and Hao Fan was likely a “happy coincidence,” but the Iranians are expected to try “all kinds of ways to get things out,” he added. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.title: 1 MW floating wave energy converter gets green light for test site deployment
articles.summary: WEDUSEA, a €19.6 million collaborative project bringing together 14 European partners, has secured a marine license that allows the installation...
articles.body: Tidal & Wave Energy November 20, 2026 · 1 minute ago 1 MW floating wave energy converter gets green light for test site deployment NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email EMEC WEDUSEA, a €19.6 million collaborative project bringing together 14 European partners, has secured a marine license that allows the installation of a 1 MW OE Buoy floating wave energy converter and associated moorings at the European Marine Energy Centre's (EMEC) test site in Orkney. Co-funded by the EU Horizon Europe Programme and Innovate UK, WEDUSEA, which brings together 14 partners from industry and academia across Ireland, the UK, France, Germany and Spain, aims to create a step change for the wave energy industry and support its progression towards commercialization. The marine license granted by the Marine Directorate, previously Marine Scotland, allows the 1 MW-rated, unmanned floating oscillating water column device, developed by OceanEnergy, to be deployed at EMEC. Its only moving part, the turbine rotor, sits on deck above the waves, while all electrical equipment is housed below deck in a sealed machine room. As waves cause air trapped within the OE Buoy hull to oscillate, the airflow drives the turbine to generate electricity. This electricity will be exported to the grid via an underwater umbilical and export cable, EMEC explained. The OE Buoy and its mooring system will be installed at Berth 5 at the Billia Croo wave energy test site. Furthermore, EMEC has developed an extensive environmental monitoring plan for the deployment, which will monitor the habitat above and below the water’s surface in the vicinity of the OE Buoy. The monitoring program will begin before installation to establish a baseline of benthic and pelagic activity in the deployment area, helping to build understanding of the marine environment before, during and following deployment. articles.body: US Coast Guard Commissions New Cutter for Caribbean Ops Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 (Credit: US Coast Guard) The U.S. Coast Guard has commissioned its newest Sentinel-class fast response cutter, USCGC Marvin Perrett (WPC 1164), during a ceremony in New Orleans, ahead of the vessel's deployment to its homeport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The commissioning ceremony took place at the Julia Street Cruise Ship Terminal, marking the cutter's official entry into active service. Following commissioning, the vessel and its crew will transit to San Juan, from where they will conduct operations across the Caribbean and the United States' southern maritime approaches. Its missions will include search and rescue, maritime law enforcement and homeland security operations. The Sentinel-class cutter is equipped with advanced maritime sensors, integrated intelligence and communications systems, and capabilities for deploying pursuit boats over the horizon. The Coast Guard said the vessel would strengthen its capacity to conduct maritime security, border protection and search and rescue missions in the region. The cutter is named after Marvin Perrett, a New Orleans native and Coast Guard veteran who operated Higgins landing craft during World War II, participating in the Normandy landings and subsequent operations in southern France and the Pacific. Perrett later received a Knight of the Legion of Honor medal from France in recognition of his wartime service.

articles.body: Cabling November 20, 2026 · 1 minute ago Nexans completes deep-water cable laying ops off Australia for Chevron NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Nexans Nexans has completed the laying and trenching of the high-voltage dynamic cable for Chevron's Jansz-Io Compression (J-IC) project offshore Western Australia. The cable-laying vessel (CLV) Nexans Aurora installed 26 buoyancy modules and trenched 30 kilometers of cable, after which it left Australia on October 23. J-IC uses subsea compression to sustain gas supply to the Gorgon LNG and domestic gas plants on Barrow Island. The 145 kV cable, about 135 kilometers long, runs from the island to a floating field control station, which powers and controls the compressors on the seabed. The completed operation included the overboarding and pull-in of the cable head to the field control station, installation of the buoyancy modules using a horizontal method developed, laying of the cable in its dynamic configuration, installation of about 200 meters of vortex-induced vibration (VIV) strakes in the Scarp section, cable lay up the Scarp, float-out and pull-in of the second cable end at Barrow Island, as-laid survey and cable trenching. Before handover, the remaining work includes cable jointing at the field control station and on Barrow Island, rock stabilization along the last 28 kilometers of the route, and final soak test, planned for February. Nexans Chevron sanctioned the Jansz-Io compression project in early July 2021 and ordered the field control station from the Daewoo Shipbuilding & Marine Engineering (DSME) shipyard, now known as Hanwha Ocean, a few months later. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 6 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Grane offshore oil platform in the North Sea, which also receives production from the Breidablikk field tied back to it Source: Equinor The growing tension between climate accountability and concerns over energy security and industry competitiveness in Europe is highlighted by two developments, which spotlight two different directions in European fossil fuel policy. Norway's Supreme Court has invalidated approvals for North Sea oil and gas fields over failures to take into account greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from burning the extracted fuels, strengthening requirements for climate assessments, while the European Union (EU) has agreed to give fossil fuel importers two additional years to comply with methane rules. The Norwegian ruling, which establishes that the climate impact of burning oil and gas needs to be assessed before petroleum projects are approved, declared the approval of plans for the development and operation (PDOs) of offshore fields invalid due to procedural errors. The case concerned the validity of approving PDOs for the Breidablikk and Tyrving fields and the Yggdrasil area, encompassing three fields in the North Sea. According to Supreme Court judgment and order of November 13, 2026, regarding appeal against Borgarting Court of Appeal's judgment and order of November 14, 2025, emissions to air were assessed, but the assessments covered only production emissions and not combustion emissions, so the environmental organizations Föreningen Greenpeace Norden (Greenpeace Nordic) and Young Friends of the Earth Norway (Natur og Ungdom) brought an action seeking declarations that the decisions were invalid due to procedural errors. The Supreme Court sitting as a grand chamber unanimously held that, under the EU Environmental Impact Assessment Directive, as implemented in Norwegian law, the combustion emissions resulting from petroleum extraction must be assessed before a PDO can be approved, which is consistent with the advisory opinion delivered by the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) Court in the case. As the EFTA Court interprets EU law, this requirement applies across the European Economic Area, not just in Norway. The Supreme Court also addressed the extent to which combustion emissions have to be assessed and held by a six-to-five majority that the environmental impact assessment needs to include both the combustion emissions from the project in question and the aggregate emissions from other existing and approved projects on the Norwegian Continental Shelf (NCS), but unanimously agreed that it is not required to address the specific consequences of the increase in temperature that may result from the combustion emissions. Related Articles Fossil Energy North Sea oil project comes on stream ahead of schedule 2 min read The same majority of six justices decided that the environmental impact assessments and the authorities’ evaluations were deficient, as they failed to take into account the aggregate emissions from existing and approved petroleum extraction projects on the NCS; thus, the approvals were declared invalid due to procedural errors. The licence holders were not parties to the case before the Supreme Court. While the fact that the approvals were declared invalid due to procedural errors in proceedings between the environmental organizations and the state does not mean that the licences automatically ceased to have effect vis-à-vis the licence holders, the Norwegian Ministry of Energy has to reconsider the matter on the basis of proper procedure, as the judgment clarifies the requirements applicable to environmental impact assessments of GHG emissions in connection with the approval of PDOs for petroleum deposits. Greenpeace has welcomed the ruling in which the Grand Chamber of Norway’s Supreme Court invalidated permits for three North Sea oil and gas fields, emphasizing that the decision deals “a severe blow” to the Norwegian state and Equinor and Aker BP , which developed the Breidablikk, Yggdrasil, and Tyrving fields. The ruling is a result of a years-long battle for Greenpeace Nordic and Young Friends of the Earth Norway. " This historic ruling changes Norwegian oil policy forever, and sets a precedent the world cannot ignore. Norway can no longer ignore the global damage caused when its oil and gas are burned abroad. Norwegian authorities are now obligated to take into account the enormous climate damage caused by Norwegian oil and gas. This is a momentous victory for global climate justice. " — Haldis Tjeldflaat Helle Norway lead in Greenpeace Nordic Related Articles Fossil Energy Norway greenlights $700 million tie-back project in North Sea 3 min read By affirming lower court rulings, the environmental organization claims that the Supreme Court set a new precedent, establishing that environmental assessments have to evaluate Scope 3 emissions, the carbon released wherever combustion takes place. The case was initiated in 2024. The decision was appealed by the Norwegian government in the Borgarting Court of Appeal and later the Norwegian Supreme Court. " The environmental organizations have won a big victory today, it’s their victory and it’s a privilege to represent them. It’s a huge Grand Chamber win today for the organizations, which will have immense existential repercussions for future generations. Today marks a victory for democracy. " — Attorney Jenny Sandvig of the law firm Simonsen Vogt Wiig, who represents the environmental organizations. In October 2025, the European Court of Human Rights confirmed that Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights requires states to assess the climate impacts of emissions from the burning of fossil fuels, including emissions generated outside their borders, before approving projects. This obligation applies to all Council of Europe members, giving the judgment far-reaching implications for fossil fuel approvals across Europe. Advertisement " This is a huge victory for today’s children who are growing up in a world fundamentally altered by climate change. Young people took the state to court, and we won. It proves that our struggle for climate justice has real force. Now, it is up to the politicians to act. " — Sigrid Hoddevik Losnegård Head of Natur og Ungdom EU delays methane rules by two years after industry pressure Meanwhile, the EU lawmakers and member states have agreed to postpone key methane requirements for fossil fuel imports until 2029, raising concerns among environmental organizations about the strength of the bloc's climate commitments. The Council of the European Union and the European Parliament reached a provisional agreement on targeted amendments to the EU methane regulation on November 19, 2026, securing a two-year postponement for the application of specific methane-related monitoring, reporting and verification obligations applicable to imports of crude oil, natural gas and coal. The move is said to provide flexibility for operators and member states to safeguard reliable and secure energy supplies amid global volatility, while upholding the EU’s commitment to reducing methane emissions in line with its climate ambitions, after EU leaders welcomed the European Commission's proposal to postpone certain obligations in the methane regulation to address the impact of the current geopolitical context on global supply chains, energy security, and energy and fuel prices. The co-legislators agreed that additional time is needed for third countries, member states, producers, importers, operators and traders to comply fully with the methane regulation, allowing them to develop the necessary implementation tools. As a result, the application of monitoring, reporting and verification obligations for natural gas, crude oil and coal importers will apply from January 1, 2029, instead of January 1, 2027, while methane-intensity reporting for both importers and EU producers will apply from August 5, 2030, instead of August 5, 2028. " Tonight, we achieved a pragmatic balance on the methane regulation, addressing the pressures in the energy market while maintaining the EU’s leadership in reducing methane emissions. This provisional agreement demonstrates the EU’s commitment to an effective approach to cutting harmful methane emissions while shielding our citizens from high energy prices. " — Darragh O’Brien Ireland’s Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment Related Articles Fossil Energy EU’s first-ever methane clampdown regulation becoming law of the land 4 min read Building on the European Council’s negotiating mandate, the co-legislators agreed that the Commission will review the effective implementation of the methane regulation by January 1, 2028, in establishing transparent and accurate measurement, reporting and verification rules and reducing methane emissions from imported fossil fuels. The review will include the availability of a sufficient number of third-party verifiers to assess the conformity of the emission reports and any potential implications for the security of supply. The provisional agreement will now have to be endorsed by the European Council and the Parliament. Afterward, the targeted amendment to the methane regulation will be formally adopted by both institutions and enter into force before the end of the year. Since methane is a powerful greenhouse gas, it is estimated to be responsible for approximately 30% of global warming, which makes its reduction crucial for achieving the EU’s climate objectives. While commenting on this decision, the Greens/EFA in the European Parliament said the EU had caved in to the fossil fuel lobby, since a majority of center-right to far-right MEPs agreed to postpone the implementation of certain parts of the methane regulation by two years even though methane emissions are responsible for about a third of global warming, with the energy sector alone accounting for 10% of the global rise in temperature. " The EU is caving in to the fossil fuel lobby and the Trump administration. While the European Commission and EU member states are pushing to include a commitment to reduce methane emissions in the final text of the global climate conference in Antalya, they are simultaneously kicking the implementation of a key instrument for achieving this down the road in Brussels. It is impossible to justify how the wasteful flaring and venting of gas should somehow enhance energy security or reduce bills for consumers, especially at a time of tight supplies and high prices. " — Jutta Paulus Greens/EFA member and former European Parliament’s lead negotiator for the methane regulation Related Articles Fossil Energy €4.5 trillion investor coalition urges EU to hold the line on methane cuts 4 min read Clean Air Taskforce emphasized that the provisional deal to delay key provisions of the EU methane regulation should not become a pause on progress. " A two-year delay doesn’t have a technical justification. Costs and security of supply were overblown arguments from the beginning, and the issues around verification and certification can be solved within the first year. Details of the deal are still emerging, and while a worst-case scenario seems to have been avoided, these delays affect the credibility of the EU legislation and deal a hard blow to the hopes of fast methane emission reductions that are our best hope to limit global warming in the short term. It is now up to the Commission and Member States to advance on implementation to ensure this delay doesn’t become a pause on progress. " — Pablo Lopez Legarreta Europe Policy Manager for Methane Pollution Prevention at CATF While the Norwegian case concerns the adequacy of environmental impact assessments, particularly the assessment of greenhouse gas emissions resulting from the eventual combustion of extracted oil and gas, the EU's methane rules address methane emissions across the fossil fuel supply chain, including production, processing, transport, and imports. Although these developments concern distinct legal and regulatory issues, both raise questions about the responsibility of the fossil fuel industry for the climate impacts associated with the extraction and supply of fossil fuels, illustrating the tensions within European climate and energy governance. While legal and regulatory frameworks increasingly seek to strengthen the accountability of fossil fuel producers and importers for their emissions, these efforts need to also be reconciled with concerns about energy security and affordability. These contrasting developments serve to emphasize the EU's broader challenge of balancing the competing objectives of the energy trilemma by finding ways to come to grips with energy security, affordability, and environmental sustainability.
